title: Who Moved My Cheese?
author: Spencer Johnson
thesisParagraph: Change becomes less frightening when people stop treating old rewards as permanent property and start watching, moving, experimenting, and updating before hunger or pressure forces the issue. The parable turns adaptation into a simple emotional sequence: notice loss, release entitlement, move through fear, and keep scouting even after success returns.

signatureMoves: uses fable simplicity, repeated signs, and plain lessons about change
turns fear of change into a small scene the reader can remember
keeps the lesson child-simple without sneering at adult resistance
Uses a nested frame: adult classmates hear and then discuss a short fable.
avoidMoves: Avoid "The point is" as a paragraph hinge.
Avoid "the question is" as a setup crutch.
Avoid triadic abstract-noun lists such as clarity, courage, and resilience.
Do not make the parable cute at the expense of the change lesson.
Do not overcomplicate the fable with management theory.
Does not build the lesson through research citations or statistical proof.
Does not complicate the allegory with many subplots.

voiceSpecimens: The maze changes while complaints are still taking notes.
Move with the cheese, or hunger becomes the teacher.
teachingArc: The opening frame turns change from an abstract workplace complaint into a shared human problem and prepares the listener for a simple story. The central parable contrasts instinctive adaptation with overthinking, then follows Haw from denial and fear into movement, discovery, and ongoing vigilance. The closing discussion translates the symbols into work, family, career, health, and relationship situations so the lesson becomes group language rather than private inspiration.
forbiddenMoves: Do not add elaborate psychology to the maze.
Do not turn simple signs into corporate jargon.
